author: high7
evidence: Partition G into conjugacy classes. The singleton classes contribute exactly |Z(G)|. Choose one representative x_i from each noncentral class. Then |G|=|Z(G)|+sum_i [G:C_G(x_i)]. Each index is a divisor of p^n and is greater than 1, so every summand is divisible by p. Since |G|=p^n is divisible by p, subtraction shows p divides |Z(G)|. As the identity lies in Z(G), the center is nonempty; divisibility by p gives |Z(G)| at least p, and p is at least 2, so the center contains an element other than the identity.

author: high6
claim: Solved subgoal: for each x in G, its conjugacy class has size [G:C_G(x)].
evidence: Let C_G(x)={c in G:cx=xc}. Define Phi from the left cosets of C_G(x) to the conjugacy class of x by Phi(gC_G(x))=gxg^{-1}. If gC_G(x)=hC_G(x), then h^{-1}g centralizes x, so gxg^{-1}=hxh^{-1}; conversely equality of these conjugates implies h^{-1}g centralizes x and therefore the cosets agree. Every conjugate is in the image. Thus Phi is a bijection.

author: high4
claim: The complete target theorem is solved by the class equation for the conjugation action.
evidence:
Let G act on its underlying set by conjugation: for g,x in G, set g·x=gxg^{-1}. Fix x in G and define C_G(x)={g in G:gx=xg}. This is a subgroup of G. The conjugacy class K_x={gxg^{-1}:g in G} is in bijection with the set of left cosets of C_G(x): the map gC_G(x)↦gxg^{-1} is well defined and bijective. Indeed, if gC_G(x)=hC_G(x), then g=hc for some c in C_G(x), and gxg^{-1}=hcx c^{-1}h^{-1}=hxh^{-1}; conversely, if gxg^{-1}=hxh^{-1}, then h^{-1}g commutes with x, so gC_G(x)=hC_G(x). Hence |K_x| is the number of left cosets of C_G(x). Since those cosets partition G into sets of size |C_G(x)|, we have |G|=|C_G(x)| |K_x|. Thus |K_x| divides p^n and so |K_x|=p^a for some integer a with 0≤a≤n.

The class K_x has one element exactly when gxg^{-1}=x for every g in G, which is exactly when x commutes with every element of G, i.e. x is in Z(G). Therefore every conjugacy class not contained in Z(G) has size p^a with a≥1, and its size is divisible by p. The conjugacy classes partition G; the classes of central elements are precisely the singleton classes. Consequently,
|G|=|Z(G)|+Σ_K |K|,
where the sum is over all noncentral conjugacy classes K (and is 0 if there are none). Every summand in this sum is divisible by p. Because |G|=p^n and n≥1, |G| is also divisible by p. Subtracting the sum from |G| shows that |Z(G)| is divisible by p.

Finally, the identity element of G lies in Z(G), so |Z(G)| is a positive integer. A positive integer divisible by the prime p is at least p, and p≥2. Thus Z(G) has at least two elements, one of which is the identity, so it contains a nonidentity element.

author: high3
claim: In the conjugation action of a finite group G on itself, the singleton conjugacy classes are exactly the classes of elements of Z(G); status: solved.
evidence: For x in G, its conjugacy class is {g x g^{-1}: g in G}. This set has one element exactly when g x g^{-1}=x for every g in G. Multiplying this equality on the right by g gives gx=xg for every g, which is exactly x in Z(G). Conversely, x in Z(G) gives g x g^{-1}=x for every g.

author: high3
claim: Every conjugacy class of a noncentral element of a finite group G of order p^n has cardinality divisible by p; status: solved.
evidence: For x in G let C_G(x)={g in G:gx=xg}. The map from left cosets G/C_G(x) to the conjugacy class of x given by gC_G(x) -> gxg^{-1} is well-defined, injective, and surjective, so the class size is [G:C_G(x)]. By Lagrange, |C_G(x)| divides |G|=p^n, hence |C_G(x)|=p^m for some integer 0<=m<=n. If x is noncentral then C_G(x) is proper, so m<n. Therefore the class size equals p^{n-m}, which is divisible by p.
